Flowering of Nicodemus
From the Superintendent
   Volume 6, Issue 3
A “Facelift” for the Roadside Park… If you are
wondering where the Nicodemus Roadside Park
recently got its major facelift, we want you to know
that this is part of a continuing partnership between
the Nicodemus T ownship Board and Nicodemus
National Historic Site.  Park maintenance staff Robert
Brogden and Josh Sharon worked tirelessly with the
paint, lumber and hardware purchased by the
Nicodemus T ownship Board to complete the repairs
just in time for the arrival of our friends attending
Homecoming.  We look forward to many more such
joint projects.
The Flowers that almost weren’t… Not long before
Homecoming, Ranger Phyllis Howard and Acting
Superintendent Felix Revello were searching the
surrounding towns in vain for the bright yellow and
orange marigolds now highlighting the planters at
the T ownship Hall.  Luckily, Felix stopped by the
Larned Greenhouse on one of his weekends back
home and found just what Phyllis needed, lots of
thriving marigolds ready for planting.  But, the
proprietor of the Larned Greenhouse refused to sell
the flowers.  Unknown to Felix, Ron Scranton, owner
of the Larned Greenhouse, just happens to be a Hill
City “Hometown Boy”.  Instead, Ron insisted that
Felix take the flowers for free, explaining that he
wanted to give the flowers for the project to express
his fond memories of the people of Nicodemus.
Phyllis planted the flowers and continues to nurture
them through the summer and fall.  Thank you
Phyllis and Ron!
We Moved! (but not very far)...  Park offices moved
from Apartment 4B in the Villas to Apartment 1B.
The new office is larger, reflecting the anticipated
addition of an Administrative T echnician to the on-
Site staff and related need for increasing our office
space.

A Brief Biography of Acting
Superintendent Felix Revello
Ranger Felix Revello has 30 years of service in a wide
variety of national parks throughout our nation.  His
latest assignment is at Fort Larned NHS, where he
serves as Chief Ranger since August 1993.  Revello has
been responsible directing ranger activities
encompassing interpretation, law enforcement, fee
collection, park safety officer and natural and cultural
resource management.  Revello was also heavily
involved with initiating operations and planning for
Nicodemus National Historic Site, which is
administratively supported by Fort Larned National
Historic Site.  In particular, he was an active participant
on the General Management Plan team, Historic
Structures Report and Cultural Landscape Report.  He
also served as Acting Superintendent for Nicodemus
National Historic Site for a total of several months.

Nicodemus National Historic Site
Welcomes Acting Superintendent
Felix Revello has been detailed as Acting
Superintendent for Nicodemus National Historic Site
to temporarily fill the vacant Superintendent
position.  Superintendents provide the overall
supervision of national parks.
Revello also currently serves as Chief Ranger of Fort
Larned National Historic Site in Larned, Kansas.  He
has served with the National Park Service for 25 +
years. His experience in the Park Service includes
parks in the United States and its territories. Such
parks as U.S. Virgin Islands National Park (Virgin
Islands), Christiansted National Historic Site (Virgin
Islands), Buck Island Reef National Monument
(Virgin Islands), Cape Lookout National Seashore
(North Carolina), Colorado National Monument
(Colorado), Grant-Kohrs Ranch National Historic
Site (Montana), and Castillo de San Marcos National
Monument (Florida), and Theodore Roosevelt
National Park (North Dakota).
Superintendent Revello was asked about his vision
for the Park. Superintendent Revello said, “T oday, the
town of Nicodemus is one of the few surviving
physical expressions of African American
contributions to our Nation’s western settlement.
Nicodemus is particularly significant in American
history for its distinction as the last surviving town
developed and settled west of the Mississippi by
African Americans during the Reconstruction era.  Its
story is of a people overcoming oppression to
participate in one of our country’s greatest
adventures.  Nicodemus symbolizes the pioneering
spirit of all African Americans coming “Out West” as
farmers, soldiers, cowboys, entrepreneurs and all of
the other roles we commonly think of as uniquely
western.  I see Nicodemus National Historic Site
keeping this exciting story fresh and alive as an
inspiration for all people.”
Nicodemus National Historic Site is located in
Nicodemus, Kansas off Highway 24, 13 miles east of
Hill City and 16 miles west of Stockton.  The visitor
center is housed in Nicodemus T ownship Hall.  Park
Rangers are available to relate site history and present
audio-visual programs.  Depending upon staff
availability, the park is usually open from 8:30 a.m. to
5:00 p.m. daily . For additional information, contact us
at 785-839-4233.  Visit us on the web at
www.nps.gov/nico .

Santa Fe T rail Rendezvous 2008
The Santa Fe T rail Center, Fort Larned National
Historic Site and the Santa Fe T rail Association would
like to invite you to the 2008 Santa Fe T rail
Rendezvous, September 18-20.
Events will be at the Santa Fe T rail Center, the Larned
Community Center and Fort Larned National
Historic Site.
This year’s focus will be on the “The Evolution of
Freighting on the Santa Fe T rail” and will examine
how freighting developed during the 60 years that
trade goods flowed along this historic route. It will
also focus on the economic, social and cultural
backgrounds of those who participated in the trade
between Missouri and Santa Fe.
Y ou can learn more about this event and find
registration form as well as local area information by
visiting Fort Larned National Historic Site website at
http://www.nps.g ov/fols.
Fort Larned National Historic Site is a free admission
park and is open seven days a week from 8:30AM to
4:30PM except Thanksgiving, Christmas, and New
Y ears Day .  Reservations can be made for guided
tours all year, advance notice required. Call 620-285-
6911.

Hello everyone – again!  After returning to my home in
Wisconsin after spending over two months as Acting
Superintendent this past spring, I was thrilled to be
offered an interview for the permanent position as
Superintendent.  When they called me to let me know I
was selected, there was no need to take time and think
about it – I accepted immediately (then I whooped and
hollered a lot!)
My family and I are so proud and excited about this
new chapter in our lives.  W e now make our home in
Hill City .  My wife Stephanie is continuing her on-line
studies through the University of Wisconsin-
Milwaukee.  Sam (17) is a senior and Ben (13) is in 7
th
grade.  Both are already on the football teams and
thoroughly enjoying small town life.
I write this the morning of my first day on the job,
overwhelmed, inspired and energized.  There is so
much to learn and so much to do.  But with the great
on-site staff of Phyllis, Robert and Michelle, I know
we’ll be able to make great strides forward with the
needed and desired projects and tasks on our plate.
Our office has moved to apartment 1B at the Villas –
just across the lawn from our previous office.  The
phone number remains the same.  Our door is always
open.  Stop by, email or call. I’m looking forward to
renewing friendships with those of you I met last spring
and building new ones as well
Mark Weaver

By Patty Rooney   InsideNPS
August 01, 2008
Mark Weaver, currently a community planner in
Midwest Region’s Rivers, T rails, and Conservation
Assistance program, duty stationed in Milwaukee, has
been selected as the new superintendent of Nicodemus
National Historic Site in Nicodemus, Kansas. He will
assume this new assignment on August 31st, replacing
Sherda Williams, who transferred in April to James A.
Garfield National Historic Site in Ohio.
“Mark’s proven ability to engage partners and
communities will serve him well in this new
assignment,” said regional director Ernest Quintana.
“W e’re very pleased to welcome him as part of our
Midwest management team.”
Weaver began his National Park Service career in 1993,
serving as a park landscape architect at Ozark National

“W e’re very pleased to welcome him as part of our
Midwest management team.”
Weaver began his National Park Service career in 1993,
serving as a park landscape architect at Ozark National
Scenic Riverways before assuming his current position
in 1998. Prior to his federal service, Weaver was a
landscape architect in Arizona, California, and
Michigan, and an assistant professor in the landscape
architecture program at Auburn University .
From April to June of 2008, W eaver had served as acting
superintendent at Nicodemus National Historic Site.
“In my short time at Nicodemus I fell in love with the
people, the place, the story and the surroundings,” said
Weaver of his springtime tenure at Nicodemus.  “Now,
with this permanent role I am even more energized to
work with the community to protect and preserve this
important piece of American history .”
An Oscoda, Michigan, native, Weaver earned his
bachelor’s of landscape architecture from Michigan
State University, and completed his master’s of
landscape architecture through Virginia Polytechnic
Institute and State University (Virginia T ech).  Mark’s
wife, Stephanie (Marshall) Weaver, is a retired pastry
chef from the Detroit area and is currently working on
her bachelor’s degree in information resources online
through the University of Wisconsin Milwaukee.  They
have two sons, Sam, 17, and Ben, 13. In their spare time,
the W eavers enjoy bicycling, travel, gardening and their
dogs.

News From Our Park Partners
At its annual awards luncheon on June 12, the Federal
Executive Association of Arkansas formally recognized
the staff of Central High School National Historic Site
in Little Rock as “Federal T eam of the Y ear” for 2008.
Superintendent Mike Madell, who nominated the park
team for the award, stated “This is a hard-working group
of individuals who continually demonstrate the
amazing accomplishments that are possible through
commitment, teamwork, and a shared vision.  It has
been, and continues to be, my honor to work with
every one of them.”
The NPS team, only 7.7 FTE in size, served as
participants, organizers, and leaders in the planning and
implementation of 50
th  Anniversary of the
Desegregation of Little Rock Central High School
special events and programming.  This included the
dedication of the park’s new visitor center, which serves
as a place to educate current and future generations
about the Little Rock desegregation crisis, the Little
Rock Nine, and civil rights in America.  The facility also
serves as an anchor in a neighborhood that has suffered
from years of disinvestment.  Through its work, the
NPS team supported the vision of the Little Rock
mayor’s 50
th Anniversary Commission to “…reflect on
the past, examine the present, and promote future
reconciliation and growth.”

by Arkansas FEA

The Crisis at Central High
On the morning of September 23, 1957, nine African
American teenagers stood up to an angry crowd
protesting integration in front of Little Rock’s Central
High as they entered the school for the first time. This
event, broadcast around the world, made Little Rock
the site of the first important test of the United State
Supreme Court’s historic Brown v. Board of Education
of T opeka  decision.  The nine African American
teenagers faced great obstacles and angry mobs in
September 1957 to desegregate Little Rock Central
High School. Ranging in ages from 15 to 17, these
teenagers showed an enormous amount of courage and
are considered civil rights activists - meaning that they
fought for the right for children all over the country to
attend the school of their choice regardless of their race.
T oday, history remembers these students as the “Little
Rock Nine.” Their actions showed the world that
individuals who act upon their beliefs can change the
course of history .  Y ou can learn more about the Little
Rock Nine by visiting Central High School National
Historic Site website at 
http://www.nps.gov/chsc/.

In addition to opening the visitor center and
supporting the 50 th Anniversary commemoration, the
NPS team maintained a high quality of service in
fulfillment of the agency mission and park purpose.
During 2007, NPS team members conducted 50
outreach programs throughout the Little Rock
community, presented 349 formal interpretive
programs, and hosted 42 onsite special events.
Park staff developed a “Junior Ranger” program for
patients at Arkansas Children’s Hospital; worked in
partnership with Coca-Cola and youth from Inter City
Futurenet (ICFN) to sell anniversary memorabilia to
benefit both the site and ICFN programs; and
collaborated with the Center High Alert Center and
Little Rock Museum Consortium respectively to
cosponsor National Night Out and Big Boo!seum (an
alternative Halloween night experience).
The NPS team partnered with NAACP to sponsor
events supporting the Daisy Bates Education Summit;
partnered with both two local radio stations to produce
and broadcast a series of more than 100 educational
vignettes; worked with the Museum of Discovery to
arrange a grant to develop an exhibit on black
education in Arkansas; partnered with the Little Rock
School District to obtain a grant to fund the first phase
of a landscape restoration project at Central High
School; collaborated to support World Fest by
developing programs to highlight human rights issues
around the world; and worked with Ball State University
and others to sponsor an “electronic field trip’ – two
live education programs that broadcast the story of
Central High School via satellite to more than 50,000
students in classrooms in 47 states and 4 foreign
countries.

“What Do Y ou Think?”
In the “Legacy of Brown v. Board of Education” gallery
is a permanent exhibit titled “What Do Y ou Think?”
The topic changes several times of year to reflect current
events in society .
This exhibit is currently featuring “School Boards,
Busing and Brown : A History of Desegregation in
Political Cartoons 1954-2006.”
Cartoons have long provided an outlet in society for
political commentary .
Even the ancient Roman catacombs contain political
cartoons in the form of graffiti. T wentieth-century
American newspapers became a forum for comment
